statement: In the 5 by 5 grid shown, three squares are shaded. What is the smallest number of further squares that must be shaded so that both dashed diagonals are lines of symmetry of the pattern?

figure.alt: A 5 by 5 grid of squares with both diagonals drawn as dashed lines. Counting rows from the top and columns from the left, three squares are shaded: row 1 column 2, row 2 column 5, and row 4 column 4. The square in row 4 column 4 lies on the diagonal from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.

choices.misconception: I only made the pattern symmetric about the diagonal from the top left to the bottom right, which needs just 2 more squares.
I only made the pattern symmetric about the diagonal from the top right to the bottom left, which needs 3 more squares.
I reflected each shaded square once in each diagonal but did not reflect the new squares again, so I missed the square opposite each one through the centre.
I thought the square lying on a diagonal needs no partner at all, so I added 3 squares for each of the other two.

hints: Reflect each shaded square in both diagonals, and keep going.

Every reflection of a shaded square in either diagonal must be shaded, and so must the reflections of those new squares. Each shaded square brings a whole group with it, and a square on a diagonal brings a smaller group.
Row 1 column 2 brings row 2 column 1, row 4 column 5 and row 5 column 4. Row 2 column 5 brings three more squares. Row 4 column 4 brings only row 2 column 2.

solutions.reliable: Count rows from the top and columns from the left. Reflecting in the diagonal from top left to bottom right swaps the row and column numbers; reflecting in the other diagonal sends row r, column c to row 6 - c, column 6 - r. Row 1 column 2 forces row 2 column 1, row 4 column 5 and row 5 column 4: 3 new squares. Row 2 column 5 forces row 5 column 2, row 1 column 4 and row 4 column 1: 3 new squares. Row 4 column 4 lies on the first diagonal and forces only row 2 column 2: 1 new square. These 10 squares reflect onto each other in both diagonals, so 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 more squares are needed and enough. The transferable idea: a symmetric pattern is made of complete groups of squares that the symmetries move onto each other.
solutions.elegant: Two reflections in the diagonals together also give a half turn, so a square that is on neither diagonal belongs to a group of 4, and a square on one diagonal (other than the centre) belongs to a group of 2. The three groups hold 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 squares, and 3 are already shaded, so 7 more are needed.

whyOnTest: Symmetry completion tests whether you keep reflecting until nothing new appears, rather than reflecting each square only once.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
